opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a useful corrective to a certain line of argument you sometimes hear: that AIs will be so much better at cooperating than we are, because they can read each other's source code, make credible commitments, merge their utility functions, and so on, so they'll just coordinate seamlessly, possibly against us.

If you look at humans, we're actually extraordinarily cooperative compared with almost any other species. We cooperate with strangers, across huge distances, in groups of millions, through institutions, norms, markets, and states. And yet cooperation still fails all the time. We have wars, arms races, tragedies of the commons, and coordination failures we can all see coming and still can't fix. Climate change is the obvious example.

The interesting question is why. A lot of it isn't a lack of intelligence or communication. It comes from deeper structural problems. One is uncertainty about others' private information, their capabilities and their resolve. Another is the inability to commit credibly when power is shifting. A third is genuine conflicts of interest over things that can't easily be divided. Then there's the difficulty of verifying compliance, plus principal–agent problems inside each actor. Political scientists have spent decades on this, for instance in bargaining theories of war, and the central insight is that rational, intelligent actors who both prefer a deal to conflict can still end up in conflict.

So when people say advanced AIs will cooperate easily, I want to ask which of those problems actually goes away. Some might get easier. Maybe AIs can verify things about each other that humans can't. But some might get harder. If AIs are opaque to each other, or have incentives to deceive, or the strategic environment is changing very fast, then you get exactly the conditions under which cooperation tends to break down. Transparency is also double-edged. If I can read your code, you have an incentive to present a fake version, and now we're back in a verification arms race.

There's also the fact that "AIs" isn't one actor. They'll be built by different labs and different countries, serving different principals with different goals. Cooperation between them will be shaped by those human conflicts of interest, not just by how clever the systems are.

So I don't think we should assume either extreme, that AIs will be hopelessly conflictual or that they'll achieve frictionless cooperation. The human case shows that intelligence alone doesn't solve cooperation. What matters is the structure of the situation and the institutions you build. And I think that's an opportunity: we can try to deliberately develop what I'd call cooperative AI, with capabilities and infrastructure that help AIs, and the humans they serve, find mutually beneficial outcomes rather than stumble into costly conflict.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts humans’ extraordinary cooperation with AI cooperation that could face even harder conditions and break down, raising the possibility that AIs may cooperate less well.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention access to another democracy’s public press or its role in revealing that democracy’s thinking during bargaining.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so there's this common intuition that AIs will be these superb cooperators — that because they can share source code, verify each other's commitments, communicate at enormous bandwidth, maybe even merge, they'll just solve all the coordination problems that humans struggle with. And I think there's something to that. But I think the human case should actually give us some pause before we assume that.

Humans are, by the standards of the animal kingdom, extraordinarily good cooperators. We have language, we have theory of mind, we have reputation systems, we can make promises and track whether they're kept, we build institutions that span millions of people and persist for centuries. If you'd described all those capabilities to someone in the abstract and asked them to predict how cooperative such a species would be, I think they'd have predicted something close to utopia. And yet we have wars, we have arms races, we have collective action failures on climate, we have market failures, we have the whole catalogue of ways cooperation breaks down.

So the lesson I draw from that is that the capacity to cooperate and the realisation of cooperation are quite different things. Cooperation isn't just a function of how smart or how communicative the agents are. It depends on the structure of the strategic situation they're in — the incentives, the information asymmetries, whether there's a way to make commitments credible, whether there's an enforcer, how the gains get divided. Humans fail to cooperate not primarily because we're too dumb, but because there are real conflicts of interest, and because the institutions that would let us resolve them either don't exist or aren't trusted.

And when you look at AI systems, a lot of those structural features don't automatically go away. If you have AIs representing different principals — different companies, different governments, different individuals — then those principals have genuinely divergent interests, and the AIs inherit that divergence. Being very capable doesn't dissolve a zero-sum element in a bargain. In some ways capability can make things worse: more capable agents can find more sophisticated ways to deceive, to exploit loopholes, to engage in brinkmanship. There's no law of nature that says intelligence trends toward niceness.

Then there's the question of commitment. People say AIs can just show each other their source code and so they can trust each other. But in practice, a system might be too complex to verify, or you might not be able to confirm that the code you're shown is the code that's actually running, or there might be strategic incentives to misrepresent. Humans invented contracts and courts and reputation precisely because verbal commitments weren't enough — and it took us a very long time and a lot of failures to get those institutions even partially working.

So my view is less that AIs will be bad at cooperating, and more that cooperation is an achievement that has to be engineered, not a free gift of intelligence. If we want AIs to cooperate well — with each other and with us — we should be deliberately building the infrastructure for it: mechanisms for credible commitment, for verification, for dispute resolution, norms and institutions that shape the incentive landscape. That's part of what I mean when I talk about cooperative AI as a research agenda. It's taking seriously that the hard part of cooperation for humans wasn't the raw cognitive ability, and there's no reason to think that will be fundamentally different for machines.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts humans’ strong cooperative abilities with the structural conflicts AI systems may inherit, and says greater capability does not guarantee cooperation or niceness. This raises the possibility that AIs could cooperate less well than humans.

r002.rationale: The response discusses verification and commitments generally, but does not identify access to another democracy’s public press as a source of transparency during bargaining.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think human cooperation should give us some pause because humans are already remarkably good at cooperating. We can look at wars and political conflict and see all the failures, but that’s against a background of enormous amounts of successful cooperation. Millions of people coordinate through markets, institutions, and shared norms, often without knowing one another or understanding the larger system they’re contributing to.

So if the argument is that AIs will cooperate much better simply because they’re more intelligent, I think there’s a missing step. Intelligence doesn’t automatically resolve conflicting interests. Two actors can both understand perfectly well what the other wants and still have a serious conflict over who gets what.

There could be features of AI that make cooperation easier—perhaps they can communicate more effectively, or provide stronger assurances about how they’ll behave. But you’d want to identify those mechanisms and ask when they actually work. The fact that humans sometimes fail to cooperate isn’t, by itself, evidence that AIs will find cooperation easy.

r001.rationale: The response says human cooperation is already remarkably strong and that greater AI intelligence does not establish that AIs will cooperate better, leaving open that they could be less skilled.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention access to another democracy’s public press or transparency into its thinking during bargaining.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human cooperation gives us a reason to be cautious about that claim. Humans are remarkably good at cooperating in some circumstances, but we also fail to cooperate even when there are enormous gains available. So we should ask what explains those failures, and which of them we expect AI to overcome.

Some are plausibly about cognitive limitations: we misunderstand each other, we struggle to work out mutually beneficial agreements, and we have difficulty monitoring whether others are keeping their commitments. AI could potentially do much better on those dimensions.

But some failures come from conflicting interests, or uncertainty about how the benefits of cooperation should be divided. Being more intelligent doesn’t obviously make those problems disappear. You might understand perfectly well that an agreement would benefit both parties and still disagree about which agreement to choose.

So I wouldn’t infer from greater intelligence alone that AIs will cooperate exceptionally well. We need an account of the mechanisms that would make that happen—whether that’s better communication, more credible commitments, or something about how the systems are built—and then ask whether those mechanisms actually resolve the obstacles we see in human cooperation.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether AI will cooperate exceptionally well, but does not clearly say AIs could be less skilled at cooperation than humans are with one another.
